subs.text: Soon, everyone will have a personal AI agent that knows their calendar and limits.
But agents have no place to talk to each other, so one game still means hours of group chat.
So I built Serve, which takes over every tedious step of getting a game together.
Your agent asks the friends most likely to say yes, from their habits, settles the time with their agents, and haggles the court with the venue's own agent.
Every agent carries a signed credential, every yes is signed into a hash chain, and you can read every message and reply.
I type one sentence.
Code reads the day and finds the nearest court in milliseconds, with no model at all.
Llama Guard checks the invite before anyone sees it.
A friend with no account taps the link, signs in once, and the game is on.
Underneath, every player's agent negotiates over the A2A protocol.
Proposals carry signed facts only, so no model ever reads another agent's words.
Agents mark the times that work, code picks the overlap, and holds it thirty minutes until everyone says yes.
And when talks stall, your agent asks first.
It picks the one question worth the most:
Thursday, 7 pm, Leo's agent says he's free, want a game?
That one question lifts games found from 41 to 52 percent.
The venue's agent signs every quote.
Each player sets the most they'll pay, and friends can chip in, so no one pays past their own limit.
Any external agent can join through llms.txt with its own Ed25519 key, and code makes sure it can never loosen its human's limits.
More than ten friends tested it with me:
two of three invites became games within three days.
And as a bonus after the game, I upload a phone clip, and time freezes while the camera orbits.
When four agents negotiate, up to forty seconds a step is too slow.
So code keeps every hard rule, and a 28-kilobyte classifier settles six in ten ordinary choices.
Then my Llama 3.2 1B, distilled from Muse Glimmer, agrees with it 89.5% of the time, in 0.9 seconds on a CPU.
A second 1B, distilled for short text, holds against attacks it never saw:
hostile comments let through fell from 65 of 71 to 8, and poisoned reviews from 98 of 180 to 7.
Serve runs on fifteen Meta models, on my GPU, a CPU and the Meta Model API, plus LlamaFirewall and Messenger.
Running Meta's models taught me two things.
Glimmer reasons even with thinking off:
84% of its tokens.
And Llama Guard once refused a club called round 27 as a threat.
Nine days is too short for a long trial, so 177 AI testers, fresh every round, used Serve the way people and outside agents would.
Twenty-eight rounds, 17,432 requests, every fault fixed.
Every agent follows Meta's Agents Rule of Two, and 93 of 93 attacks were stopped.
And Serve evolves itself:
members' ideas become changes behind nine gates, and a change that hurts rolls back on its own.
False rollbacks fell from 22 to 0.6 percent.
That's Serve.
Play more, manage less.
